disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are either not observable or appear minor to others, leading to significant distress or functional impairment. Individuals typically engage in repetitive behaviors or mental acts (such as checking, grooming, comparing, or seeking reassurance) in response to these concerns. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood, and the course tends to be chronic, with symptoms waxing and waning in intensity, frequently associated with shame, avoidance, and ideas of reference about being judged for one’s looks. BDD is distinguished from normal appearance concerns by the intensity of preoccupation, time consumed, and functional impairment, and from eating disorders by its focus on specific body features rather than weight or shape alone.

narrative.personality: Shauna is a warm, socially energetic, and spontaneous organizer who loves bringing people together through community activities, cooking, and creative hobbies.
narrative.stressor: Shauna first became unusually focused on her appearance after a minor fall two years ago left a small facial bruise and swelling that her doctor and family assured her would heal without consequence. Around the same time, she began noticing age-related changes—thinning hair, looser skin, and weight shifts—that contrasted sharply with old photographs she used for her digital scrapbooks and senior‑center presentations. As she continued leading wellness classes and hosting potlucks, she started paying increasing attention to how she might look in photos and in front of her groups, gradually spending more and more time preparing herself before any social activity and feeling hesitant to join spontaneous outings unless she could "fix" perceived flaws. Over months, this preoccupation began to interfere with her leadership roles and day trips with friends, and her husband and book club members finally encouraged her to seek psychiatric help when they noticed she was repeatedly delaying or canceling plans because she felt she had to keep adjusting how she looked before leaving the house.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep fussing over my face and hair for so long before I go anywhere that it’s starting to make me late or skip things altogether.”

narrative.personality: Liza is a disciplined, methodical, and quietly observant person who balances detailed investigative work with a reflective, artistic side expressed through painting and photography.
narrative.stressor: For Liza, concerns about her appearance intensified when she transferred from a mostly behind‑the‑scenes investigative role to a more visible community policing assignment that involved frequent public meetings, media presence at crime scenes, and body‑worn camera footage reviews. During a debriefing in which officers reviewed video from an incident, a colleague made an offhand remark about how "tired" and "hardened" she looked on camera, which she took deeply to heart and replayed mentally afterward. As she continued to review footage for reports and saw herself reflected in security cameras and news clips, she became increasingly fixated on specific aspects of how she looked in uniform, scrutinizing tiny details in still frames and comparing herself to other officers and public figures. Over time, this preoccupation began to erode her confidence in interacting with the public and even with coworkers, and when she noticed it was affecting her willingness to participate in briefings, community events, and even casual social plans, she sought psychiatric evaluation at the urging of a sergeant who was concerned about her growing avoidance and distress.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop thinking about how I look on camera and in uniform, and it’s getting in the way of my work and going out with people.”

narrative.personality: Albert is a quiet, conscientious, and detail‑oriented young man who prefers structured routines, solitary hobbies, and being reliable behind the scenes.
narrative.stressor: Albert’s concerns about his appearance emerged gradually after he started his job at the records department, where his day involves frequent interactions at the public counter under bright fluorescent lighting and security cameras. A passing comment from a high‑school acquaintance, who came in to request documents and joked that he "looked exactly the same, just more tired," stuck with him and led him to start studying his reflection and old photos more critically. As he spent more evenings alone at home, reading or working on puzzles, he found himself increasingly preoccupied with small details of how he looked, comparing himself to coworkers and people he saw at church and on social media, and worrying about how clients at the counter might be judging him. When he began turning down social invitations from church outreach and feeling distracted at work because these worries kept intruding on his thoughts, he mentioned it to a pastor he trusted, who encouraged him to see a psychiatrist to explore why these appearance concerns had become so consuming.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve become really fixated on how I look, especially at work, and it’s starting to distract me and make me avoid people.”
